introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question (1A\* or 1B\*). Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A - CAMEROON SINCE 1850.** Question One is compulsory. Answer TWO questions from this section. Answer 1A\* or 1B\* and any other question from this section.

**1B\* (Starred question)**

Study the following extract on political developments in Southern Cameroons in the 1950s and 60s and then answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub-question is indicated in the brackets.)

**EXTRACT A**

> Yesterday representatives of the people of the Eastern Region by 45 votes to 32 rejected Cameroon representation in the Executive Council when they turned down the Cameroon's Minister, S.T. Muna, to the Regional Executive Council. We your elected representatives consider this act to be a deliberate disregard for the wishes and aspirations of the people of the Cameroons. We have therefore broken our connection with the Eastern Region because we believe that, as a minority group in the Eastern Regional Legislature, we are unable **[line 5]** to make the wishes of Cameroons people respected. We consider that our immediate duty now is to press our demand for a separate Region and to this end we call upon all Cameroonians to be prepared to make sacrifices. We strongly advise all the people of the Cameroons to boycott any future elections in the Eastern House ...
>
> All native Authorities, tribal organisations, chiefs and people of every village and town are required to send two representatives each to a conference to be held in Mamfe on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, 22, 23, 24 May **[line 10]** 1953."

**EXTRACT B**

> The Kamerun National Congress (KNC) was the first major political party in Southern Cameroons. It was created from a merger of two pressure groups. Its motto was "towards self-government or independence for united Cameroon. The great KNC party did not last long and began to show cracks after two years of its birth. **[line 15]** In 1955 Foncha and AN Jua broke away from the KNC and formed the Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP). They called for secession from Nigeria and later reunification with French Cameroon. In 1959 Foncha's KNDP party won and he became Premier.
>
> By 1961, there was no consensus as to the political future of Southern Cameroons because the politicians were deeply divided and opposed to each other. For this reason, the future of the territory could only be determined **[line 20]** by a plebiscite. The KNDP under Foncha which campaigned for independence and reunification with the Republic of Cameroon won. In June 1961, Foncha organised an All Bamenda Party conference to discuss the territory's constitutional proposals before they left for Foumban to meet the Government of the Republic of Cameroon for constitutional talks. On 1st October, Southern Cameroons was proclaimed an independent country and reunited with the Republic of Cameroon to form the Federal Republic of Cameroon. **[line 25]**

*Source: Cameroon History in the 19th and 20th Centuries by Tazifor Tajoche.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) In which year did the Eastern Regional Crisis break out? (line 1)
(ii) What name did the authors of the group that published this petition and invitation adopt? (line 3)
(iii) Give the name of the leader of this group as well as one of its members.
(iv) How many representatives from Southern Cameroon were elected into the Eastern Regional Legislature as mentioned in line 3?

(1+1+1+1=4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) 1953 [1 mark].** The extract itself dates the Mamfe conference to 22-24 May 1953, immediately after the walk-out, so the crisis broke out in 1953.

**(ii) The Cameroons Elected Members [1 mark].** The authors were the elected representatives of the Southern Cameroons in the Eastern House of Assembly at Enugu, who signed as "your elected representatives" (the group is usually described as the Southern Cameroons elected members).

**(iii) Leader: Dr E. M. L. Endeley; one member [1 mark].** Dr Emmanuel Mbella Lifafa Endeley, leader of the KNC, led the elected members. Members included N. N. Mbile (accept any named elected member from the Southern Cameroons).

**(iv) Thirteen (13) [1 mark].** Under the 1951 Macpherson constitution the Southern Cameroons sent thirteen members to the Eastern House of Assembly, where they remained a small minority among the many Eastern Nigerian members.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Give **one** importance of the Mamfe Conference of 1953 to the future political development of Southern Cameroons. (lines 10)
(ii) Outline any **two** important resolutions arrived during the conference mentioned in (b) i above.

(1+2=3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One importance [1 mark].** The Mamfe Conference united Southern Cameroons leaders behind a common demand for a separate status outside the Eastern Region; it led to the constitutional talks in London (1953) and Lagos (1954), and to the quasi-federal status granted in 1954, with the Southern Cameroons given its own House of Assembly and executive. It therefore marked the beginning of a separate political identity for the Southern Cameroons.

**(ii) Any two resolutions [1 mark each].**
1. The Southern Cameroons should be separated from the Eastern Region (no more control from Enugu).
2. The Southern Cameroons should have its own region, with its own legislature and government, within the Federation of Nigeria.
3. The elected members should continue to boycott the Eastern House of Assembly until the demand was met (as announced in Extract A).
4. A delegation should present the demand at the constitutional conferences.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Name **one** founding member of the KNC party. (line 13)
(ii) State **any two** aims of the KNC at the time of its creation. (line 13)
(iii) State **one** reason which caused people to break away from the KNC. (line 16)

(1+2+1=4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One founding member [1 mark].** Dr E. M. L. Endeley (also acceptable: N. N. Mbile, P. M. Kale). The KNC was formed in 1951 at Kumba from the merger of two pressure groups, the Cameroons Youth League and the Cameroons National Federation.

**(ii) Any two aims [1 mark each].**
1. Self-government for the Southern Cameroons (or independence for a united Cameroon, as in the motto quoted in line 13).
2. To separate the Southern Cameroons from the Eastern Region of Nigeria and have its own status.
3. To end colonial rule and defend the interests of the Cameroonians (for example against land alienation).
4. To work for the reunification of the Cameroons.

**(iii) One reason [1 mark].** Disagreement about the future of the territory: Foncha and Jua felt that Endeley was too close to Nigeria and did not push for reunification with French Cameroon (also: personal rivalry and a struggle for leadership of the party).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) State **one** benefit of the granting of a full regional status to Southern Cameroonians in 1959.
(ii) Give the exact date the plebiscite was held in British Cameroons. (line 21)
(iii) Write down the **two** plebiscite questions proposed on the Southern Cameroons electorate by the United Nations Organisation.

(1+1+2=4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One benefit [1 mark].** The Southern Cameroons obtained its own government and legislature (a Premier, an Executive Council and a House of Assembly at Buea), so it could take decisions on local matters, the Cameroonians were no longer ruled from Enugu or Lagos, and local people gained experience in self-government before the plebiscite. (Other acceptable benefits: greater control of local revenue, more Cameroonians in the civil service, new elections in 1959.)

**(ii) 11 February 1961 [1 mark].**

**(iii) The two plebiscite questions [1 mark each].** The United Nations offered the voters two alternatives:
1. *Do you wish to achieve independence by joining the independent Federation of Nigeria?*
2. *Do you wish to achieve independence by joining the independent Republic of Cameroun?*
(Independence on its own was not offered as a third choice.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) The text you are studying is about representation in public life and the promotion of national unity;
(i) Give **two** reasons why it is important to have representatives at any level of the community or nation.
(ii) Give **one** way by which you can be made a representative in your community.
(iii) State **two** ways by which national unity is practiced in your community.

(2+1+2=5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Civic-education question: a model answer is given, any valid local example is accepted.*

**(i) Any two reasons [1 mark each].**
1. Representatives carry the needs and views of the people to the authorities, so that decisions take account of the community.
2. They take part in making laws and decisions on behalf of the people who cannot all be present, which is the basis of democracy.
3. They help the community obtain development projects (roads, schools, water) and follow up their execution.
4. They help settle disputes and keep a link between the people and the government.

**(ii) One way [1 mark].** By election: the people vote for the candidate they trust (for example a councillor, a deputy, or a class or association leader). (Also: selection by the traditional council or by consensus in a village association.)

**(iii) Any two ways [1 mark each].**
1. Celebrating the National Day (20 May) and other national events together, with parades and the national anthem.
2. Living and working together across ethnic and language groups, including intermarriage and mixed neighbourhoods and schools.
3. Using both official languages (English and French) in public life and encouraging bilingualism.
4. Joint community projects, sports and cultural festivals open to every group.
